definition: ICT's view that price is delivered to serve smart money; retail stops and orders are its liquidity.
Interbank Price Delivery Algorithm: ICT's term for the price engine that references 20/40/60-day data ranges.
Buy-side liquidity (buy stops above highs) and sell-side liquidity (sell stops below lows).
Inside the range: OBs, FVGs and voids (entries). Outside the range: stops beyond its high or low (exits).
50% of the current dealing range: fair value.
Optimal trade entry: the 62–79% retracement, with 70.5% as the sweet spot.
Above / below equilibrium. Sell in premium, buy in discount.
Premium/discount array: any institutional reference level (OB, FVG, breaker, void, rejection block, old high or low).
The last opposite-close candle before a displacement, validated when price trades through its high (bullish) or low (bearish).
50% of an order block's body.
An order block that failed after a stop run and structure break; it flips role.
A level where trapped smart-money positions are closed at break-even, often followed by an explosive move.
An OB used during the decline (market maker buy model) that gets bought again as the market rises.
A three-candle range where only one side was offered: the left candle's low to the right candle's high (bearish case).
Long one-sided candles with little overlap; price tends to come back and fill them.
Wick zone at a swing extreme, from the highest (or lowest) body to the wick.
A candle that re-tests an OB and propels price; very sensitive, with tight stops.
A gap from news or a session open; price usually returns to fill it.
A false break of an old high or low (named after the Turtle traders' 20-day breakouts).
A time-of-day false move against the day's direction, after midnight NY or after 7:00 NY.
The daily candle's open, high, low and close: buy below the open on a bullish day and exit near the close.
A high-probability session window: London open, New York open, London close.
Smart money technique: correlated markets fail to confirm each other (DXY vs a pair, EUR/USD vs GBP/USD, notes vs DXY).
Pending orders in the 60-day look-back and 60-day forward window; fund-level stops.
The major change in direction or condition that ICT says happens every 3–4 months.
30-year bond, 10-year note and 5-year note futures; a failure swing in one marks a shift.
Big money defending a swing: immediate reaction at its order blocks, with displacement on the higher timeframe.
A move with the higher-timeframe flow through easy stops / a move against defended levels.
The sell side of the curve into a higher-timeframe level, then the buy side back up (or the reverse).
A strong, energetic move that leaves imbalances, showing large-player participation.
A retest that fails to make a new high or low; one of ICT's two ways the market turns.
Total open futures contracts. ICT reads a ≥15% drop at support as the liquidity provider covering (bullish).
40- and 15-year futures averages by month; a roadmap, not a signal.
Profit or loss measured in units of initial risk (3R = three times what you risked).
